blocks.x: Okay the machine is going and we're at 600 Charter Street on June the 29th 1960 and your name is? Abby Foster. Abby Foster. Abby Chiney Foster. Chiney is your nickname. That's my music name. Your music name. How did you get that name? Well the fish start to call it. Can you tell us just where you were born and when? 1914 St. Philip Street. 914 St. Philip Street. Right in St. Philip Street over near Burgundy Street. Between Burgundy and Dolphin.
He was held by a trombone.
That's George Washington.
Yeah, same size as me.
I know he played with Buddy Petit. Buddy Petit, yeah.
He's out in Los Angeles now.

Did you play with Buddy Petit very much? Yeah, I played with them. I have these records over here, these old Celestan records. Do you remember that first date, the one that they had the black rag and the tuxedo rag and careless love? About when was that made?

Can you remember who else was on that? Who was the piano player? Can you remember? Some people say that Emma Barrett played and Manuel Moneta thinks he made one date. I think Manuel did. It was Manuel Moneta on that date. He thought he made those. He said one date. Yeah, he was. Somehow Emma didn't play that day. I don't know what happened. Those were those three records. We'll play that record and then if you have any remarks to make while the record, you can tell about how we're playing it or any time after. I'll just turn it on and this will pick it up I think alright too. This is the Careless Love. I mean this is the one where you use your bristles, slide bristles. dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear
Very close.

At that time, the drum wouldn't record on the record. Only the cymbal. Only the cymbal. It wouldn't record. It would make a blank, a claw on the record. At that time, that's why it would hear the electronic blocks, the wood block. The drum wouldn't record. That's why I'm coming.
Shots behind you.
Yeah.
You can hear the blocks very rough down. You can hear the blocks very rough down. Yeah. You can hear the blocks very rough down. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. That's a good man.
That's Lars Murara. Ruh! Good.
Simon was on bass, right?

Okay, we'll try the other one with two other numbers. Did they make more than those three numbers? Only three of them came out. One called the original tuxedo rag. This one's the black rag. Do you remember if they made more than that?

Yeah, we did. Did you? Yeah. You see, on that line up, yeah, well, on this line up, we got three different men on that line up. Yeah. On this line up, we have this boy Paggio on tenor. Paul Barnes on alto, on this tape, on this one, yeah. Shots on the second trumpet. Celestane on first one.

And then John Marrero and Simon Marrero. Yeah. And Manuel Manetta on piano. On piano. Let's play this black rag, and then if you have anything else you can add to it, we can... This is the one called black rag. Originally it was trombone. Yeah. This is made in famous? This one here. Who wrote this, do you remember? Yeah, well, uh... Is this one of your original compositions there for the band? No, the real name is the band. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. The other name is Down Home Rack. Oh, it's the Down Home Rack.
It's like the Down Home Rack. Who decided to call it something different? Huh?
Who called it something different? Well, I guess they changed the name of their own song.
Maybe the record company might have come down.

Yeah, they suggested that. They claim that they had another record to another piece that should go like that some years back. See, they changed that name off because they got parts of it that sounded like the other one.
Yeah, I remember it.
That's why the man told me to stop. I'm making too much noise on the record.
You didn't play at all in that banjo chorus. Manetta told you that? Huh? Manetta told you that?
No. The recording man. The recording man. He told him, don't play too loud. Who's that? Oh? That's Paul Vaughn. Paul Vaughn, Sidney Correa, and... ... places. Man on that too. Man on that too.
Man on that too.
Man on that too. Man on that too. Man on that too. dear . You see? That's why they changed that name. Mama loves shortening bread.
Shortening Mama. Shortening bread. Yeah. See?

The company is the one that called it Black Rag. Yeah. Nothing like nothing. See what we used to call it? Down Home Rag. Yeah. See? Cause that's an old fuck number, you know? Like people used to do things in slavery times.
On the label they put William Ridgely as composer. Yeah. Oh, it says playing at Spanish Fort. Were you all working at Spanish Fort?
Yeah, Spanish Fort there. Trench in.
Trench in. Is that the same place that P. Rone played later? Yeah, that's right. No, he played that before.
He played before? Before. We went to Apple. You recorded in the fort? Huh? Where were you recording? No, we was playing at the Spanish Fort.
Where did they make the record, by the way? Huh? Where was the record made? Did they have a studio?
Yeah, that gotcha was done.
Well, that's the gotcha. Gotcha. Yeah. Here's the other number, they only put out three of those numbers. This is called Original Tuxedo Rag.
This is a good indication of what the band sounded like. Sounded like that time. Sounded like that.
Sounded like that time. Sounded like it sounded like that time. On the jobs too. On the job. Moreira strokes right with your blocks.
More of strokes right with your blocks. Right on the block.
Well it's the practice thing.
Did you work that out?

Well see we always practiced bass, bass violin, drum and banjo. Worked the same thing. Stoked the very same thing. Same thing. Practice. That's a resident. A bit of a resident. I see those other records we record that after we broke the band up.
Oh yes, Columbia. Yeah.
I saw a stand. I saw a stand. Yeah. I saw a stand. Yeah. I saw a stand.
Yeah. I saw a stand. Yeah. I saw a stand. I saw a stand. I saw a stand. I saw a stand. I saw a stand. I saw a stand. I saw a stand. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Our band. Oh yeah, we had some records. Well they used to follow us all the time, you know. And anything that we wanted in the line instrument, we didn't have to pay for it, they'd give it to us.
And that was the man of the D.H. Holmes?
One of the sons, the president's son.
A lot of people.
Well they used to like our band, you know. At that time.
I don't have any of those Columbia records here, the later ones.

And you see, well, we had a lot of friends, you know what I mean? Yeah. Well they used to, anything that we said we wanted, well they had to fix that, and all we had to do is just go to the store and tell them the charges to Mr. So-and-so. No kidding. Well it was all them boys, you know, they just were having fun. They wasn't playing for no living, they just were having fun like that, you see. Now he gave me a symbol there, it cost $65 at that time. See, well I imagine right now, I imagine right now, that symbol that he gave me was somewhere around about $150 or $165.
Everything's doubled in price now.
Because at that time I used to could get a good symbol for $16. That symbol that cost $65. That is a symbol that comes from Germany.
Oh, Germany. Was it Germany or Turkey? I thought they came from Turkey, some of them.
Well this one had a special belt and it comes from Germany. It was beat out, it was not a mold at all.
So Zildjian wasn't making symbols then, was it?
No, it wasn't mold, it wasn't, you know, mold out, it was beat out by the hammer. Pound it out, you could see the hammer marks.
Yeah, I've seen some of those old ones, yeah.
Well I was the first one had one of those.
Yeah.
It's a U.S. Evans, living in St. Charles and Belmont, gave me that for a present.
Well what else did you have in the way of, what kind of a wood block, how big was it about?
About the size.
About eight, five inch.
Yeah. About five inch. Is it wood or China? No, wood. Wood.
And did you ever use any cowbells?
Cowbells, yeah. Yeah, I used the cowbell.
Did you have?
The cowbell is a crash symbol and a Turkish symbol.
And one big Turkish and one Chinese crash symbol. Exactly, yes.
I also used a small Chinese tum tum.
Oh yes, how many, one tum tum? One tum. So just the one. And your bass drum was always 28 inches, a big 28 inch?
28 inches, oh either 28 inch or 26, sometime I would change, you know.
Yeah. Did you ever play much in parades on the street?
Parades, yeah, oh yeah.
Which bands did you work with on the street?
Tuxedas and Onward.
Onward, yeah. Who else was in the Onward band, can you remember?
Manuel Perez.
Is he the leader?
Yeah, he was the leader of that band, Manuel Perez, Unarmer Twier, and Andrew Kimball.
Oh yeah. Remember who the trombones were?
Buddy Johnson. Buddy Johnson and George Field.
Oh yeah.
Buddy Johnson and George Field. Also Paul Barberan's father.
Well you mentioned you worked quite a few jobs with him. Yeah, yeah.
And that was before the tuxedo's time. Yes.
Who was the clarinet? Do you remember?
Lorenzo Teo.
Lorenzo Teo.
Old man Barberan Alto and old man Adolph Alexander Sr. On the baritone. Yeah, baritone.

Who was the bass drum? Did you play bass drum or snare? Snare drum. Who was the bass? Heinrich Trapani. Hermes Trapani. Yeah. Yeah. The tuxedo band when they were on the street, did you wear the tuxedo uniforms then or not?
No, we wear the regular brass band. Brass band.
I didn't know if they...
We just wore the tuxedo suits to represent our name and the orchestra.
Somebody told me they wore them on the street too sometimes. Did you ever do it on the street?
No, no.
Never. Somebody told me wrong then on that one.
Well we wore them on the street when we'd be advertising, you know, playing for a dance like that.
Something like that. But I mean for parades.
But not for a parade.
I wondered. I thought it sounded a little bit funny. I didn't. But they might have done it just to...
Oh, we'll wear them to advertise. Special stuff.
Right. Who else was in the brass band? The tuxedo brass band then? Celestan and Richie?
The whole tuxedo town? The whole brass band? Yes.
If you can remember some of them.

Well, it was consisted of... ...Risley... ...and Sonny Henry. Sonny Henry? Those were the two trombone players. Eddie Jackson on... Tuba? ...Sousa Pond. Yeah. And Old Man Barbaran on alto. And Old Man Adolph Alexander on baritone.
Did he play both sometime in the tuxedo and sometime in the onward band? Yeah.

Yeah, he played with both of them. See, in other words he played with the onward band before he did the tuxedo. See, tuxedos came after the onward band. I see. See, the onward band is an older band than the tuxedo one. Yeah, that's right. So after the onward band broke up, well, those tuxedos came in. See, well, Old Man Barbaran and Old Man Alexander, well, they joined the tuxedo band. Yeah. And they made the tuxedo band. Celestan on trumpet, beat the Polkhoz on trumpet, Louis Armstrong on trumpet. Oh, yeah.
Three trubbles. How did Louis sound in those days? Oh, it was all right.
Good? It was a boy. That a boy, that's what helped make that, to see the band. Yeah.
Yeah. Did you ever play with Joe Oliver or any of those? Oh, yeah.
I played with Joe Oliver quite a while. In Ory's band. So in Kid Ory's band.
Yeah, Kid Ory's band. Okay. I know, as Ory told me once, he used to use Henry Martin on drums too some. On drums, yeah. But not all the time.
Yeah, I see, uh, in those times before his feet got bad. But then you had another fella named Happy. Oh, yes, that's right.
I've heard of him. Red Happy, huh? Red Happy.
I see, and then after, well, when Happy got together, well, it was hard to tell who was who. Some say I was the best, some say he was the best.
Was Wade unclarated at that time?
Wade, yeah, he was unclarated at that time.
Yeah. You remember when Johnny Dodds came in the band or did Punch play with Ory too, didn't he a while?
Yeah, Punch played with Ory a while before he went with Jack Kelly.
Mm-hmm. Yeah.
Then he sub the tooth a while after, you know, until he got a record.
You remember when Johnny Dodds was in Ory's band, did he play with same time you did or?
Yeah, same time I did. Same time I did.
Wade had gone when you were playing with him or was he, did he play with Wade too with that group?
No, Wade hadn't left. He left first.
Yeah. Yeah.
Then he came back. Joe Oliver left and he sent for Johnny Dodds. See? All right. That time, when Lewis was playing with Ory.
Oh, yeah.

And when he left Ory, he went out on the boat. Mm-hmm. That's why he learned to raise his music out on the boat. See? But that time, Wade had come back and started playing with Ory. Mm-hmm. Because Joe Oliver had left way a long time before, before Ory then. Yeah. After Ory went to California, well then they all hooked up together and made the band up over again after they got over there. Oh, yeah. Yeah, that's where Joe Oliver got the name of King Oliver after he got up there. But over here, this is called Joe Oliver. Yeah.
Did you ever play many of the places in the district? Did you ever play at that old tuxedo dance hall? Yeah.
Played at the tuxedo hall. That's when the boys made the band up. But Ernest Opanyo was the head drummer.
The drummer first. See?

In other words, Ernest Opanyo was always the original drum player of the tuxedo band. After they come out from there, well, they played out the field a while and they went to Jack Sheen. Yeah. So after they come back from there, after the engagement finished out with Jack Sheen, well, his feet commence to going back. Well, he tried to get me, but he couldn't get me, so he got Henry Zeno. Oh, yeah. Happened to Henry Zeno, he didn't play anymore in about five months. And he died and I went over and took the play.
Wasn't Al Nicholas with Ory about the time you were with Ory?
Alvin Nicholas?
Yeah.
No.
He was on of the questions.
He was, uh, no, he was with Joe Oliver. Oh, yeah. See, there were two different bands.
Nicholas, I think, played up at the Tom Anderson's, didn't he? Yeah, with Lois Humphrey.
With Lois Humphrey.
And Lois Humphrey. And Lois Humphrey. And Lois Humphrey, I think, was the trumpet player of the wild too.

He was the trumpet player of the wild too. Yeah. See, uh, Lois, when Lois come off of the boat, well, he took, uh, Lois Humphrey his place. Yeah. Lois Humphrey was there before Lois. When Lois left the boat, him and Sidney Desby made up a band. But it didn't last long. Sidney Desby left trumpet and went to playing trombone. Oh, yeah. But that band didn't last no more than about a year. Not quite a year. Yeah.
Tio himself, uh, had about two styles, didn't he, that he used? Two distinct styles of Tio. Tio?
Yeah. Oh, yeah. Yeah, Tio.
I mean, some of the styles we heard on the records wasn't the kind he played all the time, was it?
No. Well, he played caught in the high field. Oh, yeah. Caught in the high field. If he was feeling good, he played good. If he was, if he just feel bad, he...
Yeah, I guess a lot of people are that way. Yeah.
You had to catch him caught in the high field. That's why we used to call him Lazy Mexican.
Oh, yeah.
Cause he played caught in the East field. We used to call him Lazy Mexican for a nickname.
Do you know if that family came from Mexico really or not? Did they...
Well, really I could not say that. Mm-hmm.
Some people have told me that the old man, uh, Louie Tio and, uh, Lorenzo Senior came from Mexico.
Well, I'll tell you who, who, who should be able to tell you about that. Manu Mineta should be able to tell you about that.
He didn't seem to remember for sure. He played with the Papa Tio too at the Tuxedo Band too. Yeah. Four year time he even played there I think. Oh, yeah. He didn't remember they came from Mexico.
He can't remember that part back.
But, uh, Mr. Paul Goliere, you know. Yeah, he should know too. He said he thought they came from Mexico. He studied with the Tio.

Well, if he told you, well... He should know. Well, he should know, yeah. Yeah. His sister used to teach me, you know. I said, take lessons, I'll just go to... We call him Guy Kelly, but his right name is Edgar Kelly. Guy Kelly.
That wasn't Spider.
No, that's not Spider. That's two different man talk.
Everyone ever talks about Spider said he was really good on the jump stuff.

Yeah, yeah. Well, that's what I'm talking about. Yeah. He wasn't much of a musician. Yeah. You know what I mean? He could play it. Now, don't get me wrong. Yeah, yeah. He could play it, but I mean his reading ability wasn't so far. He could play. All right, nobody tell you he couldn't play. He really could play.
I'm wondering to continue on with your life if there's any more about Celestan's band. You say you went back to them after 1926 or so and joined Celestan's band.
Yeah, I joined back with them in the 26th.
Who was with him then? Was Schatz with him still with him then or did he have a different trumpet?
No, I was with him. We didn't have, we only had one trumpet.
Just the one trumpet?
One trumpet.
Once Ricard Alexis joined. Well, he made a record with us. He didn't play all the time?
No, not a record with the band. Edgar Keller.
Oh, he was with him then. Edgar Keller. Yeah. He's the one they call Guy Keller. Guy Keller.
He said we just used shot to make those records. Yeah. We wasn't using two trumpets at that time.
Not for the record time?
Not till after we made those records. Ricard made those last three records with him. Yeah.

Were you playing the style of the dances that you played on that record? On the records with Ricard, Alexis? Yeah. That was the style they were using in the dance hall too? Yeah. That was on the records? You used your full drum set then on the late records?
Full drum set. Yeah, on the late records. That's why you can hear the cymbals on that. Yeah.
Some of the Mareros, they stayed with the band, didn't they? Simon and uh... Simon and John.
John was the banjo player. Simon was the bass violin player. Yeah.
Who was the piano then? Jeanette Sullivan.
Jeanette Sullivan.
Jeanette. Did uh... Emma Barrett play with you much at different times?

She didn't play with us no. The second time I came back, she was playing with Ridgely. She stayed with Ridgely. She had two tuxedo band, had number one and number two. Ridgely took one part, Celestine took the other part.
Yeah, it's always confusing to me to know who was...
Well, on the last records it was Jeanette Sullivan playing piano.
Um... How long did you stay with Celestine then?
Stayed to him up until 1930.
Up until 1930. Uh... Did you uh... Go to any other band then or when did you uh... Stop playing? I know you don't play much now, do you?
But... Uh... I stopped for two years. About two years? And I went with the band of band.
Yeah.
That's why I met Bunk in U. R. Berry. Yes. After the band, after I left the band of band and uh... This uh... The fella that got killed, the band Thomas.
Did that be about 1932 then or a little bit before or when? 1932, yeah.
1932. Last part of 1932. Last part of 1932.
Last part. And how long did you stay with them? You told us a little bit about it before.
Uh... Uh... Well the band, well...
After you broke up you say you reorganized it some and...

No, well we organized the band uh... Uh... What uh... The band had. Yeah. See? He had a band before used to call uh... Black Devil. See? Well he broke up the Black Devil band to go with the Banner band. Yeah. So when he left the Banner band, he and I reorganized the Black Devil band.
Yeah.

I see. See? And that's why Bunk, we meets Bunk on the road. Yeah. We meet Bunk in Alexandria. So Bunk joined the band with us in Alexandria. See? Our headquarters were in Crowley. Yes. And so after the band... Well... The band didn't play it over five jobs was before he got killed.
So it didn't last long then. Yeah.
As soon as that old grudge the fella had against him.
Yeah. George Lewis told us all about that. Yeah. So I have that story down pretty good I think. Yeah. But uh... What did you do then after that? Come back to the city here or?
Yeah, I came back to the city. Uh...
Who did you play with? Do you remember any?
Well, things commenced getting kind of dull. Depression commenced coming in. We was playing with anybody we could.
Did you ever play in that big WPA band?
No, never did. You never did? Never did play with that. Was always lucking up to having three, four nights job. Yeah. Didn't have to... Didn't have to bottom.
Oh, you mentioned you played a little bit with Buddy Petit? Oh yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. When I was a little kid. Okay. Then I played a couple of jobs with him. But I never played... I never was a real member of them. Never a regular member. But you know our bands do. Swap up men like that.
Yeah.
You played with Deucey?
Huh?
Frankie Deucey? Yeah. I played with them also. Not regular.
Never played with Chris Kelly at any time. Yeah.
Yeah. My mama put Chris Kelly in jail twice for keeping me out all night.
I was speaking with his son just a moment ago before I came here.
Sitting out in the border guard square right by the other door.
I've never met his son. Yeah. But someday we'll talk to him too. Yeah.
He could remember.
But he doesn't know nothing about it. He doesn't know much about his father you don't think? No.
No. See, well that's the reason why I know. Because I was supposed to christen him. You understand? Well he was quite a little bit of kid when his daddy died.
Well, do you know if Buddy Petit has any relatives? Somebody, Bunk used to say he had a brother. Well he's got a son.
Yeah, he's got a brother. What have you called him?
Sonny. Sonny.
Sonny.
Do you think he's ever around? Do you ever see him anyplace?
I can put my hand on him any time. You can?
Good. I'd like to meet him someday.
Well, I'll tell you what I'll do. I knew his stepfather.
He don't live far from here.
You don't live far from here?
No, he don't live far from here. I'd like to meet him sometime because he would probably remember something about his brother.
Yeah. I'll try to bring him around as soon as possible.
Sometime. If I'm not here, sometime I'm gone you can just put his name and address on a little slip of paper and put it in the mail slot.
I'm more than happy to see him or to see him.

I'd like to run into him sometime and then I could be glad to go to his house too. He usually interviews people out at the homes of the musicians and it's a little bit noisy in here with all the traffic going by and the fire engines today.
Do you remember much about Frank Matthew? Frank Matthew? Yeah. He led a band at the Tivoli in Mexico with Charlie Love, Deucin.
Frank Goody. No, I don't know him. I know Bibb Matthews, Bill Matthews.
These guys are all brothers. All brothers, yeah.
I think there's a bunch of, come on, Bill Matthews, Bibb Matthews, and Freeman. I think they got another one, I can't call his name.
Yeah, another younger one, I think didn't take up music they told me.
Yeah, that's the one I can't call his name.

Bill Matthews played drums for the funeral the other day. For the funeral, yeah, for Barbaran's funeral. Just at Barbaran's funeral, yeah. I'm surprised he hadn't played drums for many years, he said.
Oh yeah, it's been quite a while since he played.

And on trombone all the time. Trombone. Are there any other jobs that you can think of during the Depression that you had that lasted any time at all? I guess most of them were just a few nights at a time, but any special bands that you played with?
Well, it was most get together bands.
Yeah.

I played up at Black Gold, Seven and Howard. I played out there for Miss Normandale, St. Mary and Constance. I played at Paradise and Philly and Rampart. I thought it was anybody higher, you know. Yeah, bands commenced to breaking up like that. Which I left the Depression got over, but then the bands started to making up again.
What did you do after that time?
I didn't do nothing.
You just didn't play at all? I didn't play at all. You didn't play any during the 40s?
Yeah, I played in the 40s. I play now and then relief work, you understand what I mean?
How long has it been since you've been in music now that you've been playing drums?
I've been in two years now.

About two years now. Two years. I never did get to hear you. Maybe I heard you sometime and didn't know it in the old days, but not that I remember though. Seeing you or hearing you before. But I know Bunk always wanted to get you in around 1946 or so. He was hoping to get a band together with you.
Well, I tell you, I never would stay in one place, you know.
Did you ever, where did you travel? Did you get north to Chicago ever or New York or any place, anytime?
Well, I got as boys, Minnesota. Did you really?
You got to? Minnesota.
I got as boys in Minnesota and I got as boys in St. Louis.
Ever get to California?
No, never get there.
Never did get there?
No, I was supposed to go there, but I never did.
Were you with Silstan when Clem Rabin played with him? Yeah. Did Clem sound very much like Piku or?
Well, I wouldn't say.
No.
I said Piku played all together, a different style from them all together.
Well, was Ramon a popular clarinetist in town at that time? Well, Piku was the most popular time. Yeah. Cool. I just wondered because he's out in San Francisco, we're going to have him in the court.
Who were some of the other better clarinetists? You mentioned Charlie McCurdy. How did he play?
He was a number one. He was a number one musician. A number one musician. What I mean by A number one, no sooner they put a piece up in front of him, he don't have to rehearse it.
I know Bunk said he was very good, one of the best. Yeah. George Boccage, did you ever know him or play with him? Yeah.

Yeah. He was a great clarinet player too. Him and Lorenzo Teo on the same style. Played when they got ready. I don't say that they couldn't play. When they played like nothing, well, they just wasn't feeling good. But when they got ready to play, nobody couldn't touch them, black or white.
Boccage was in the Onward band, wasn't he?

Charles Boccage, yeah. You see those fellas like that, those fellas in Manu Peris's time, like I was telling you, like Manu Peris's time and Peter Boccage, Manu Mineta, those fellas are all about the same age. All about the same. Freddie Keppert and them, all those.
I was going to ask you, did you ever play with Freddie Keppert?
Yeah, I played with him, but not a regular man.
Yeah, not a regular.
Yeah.
He went away from here from pretty young parents. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

You mean Chiney played with you, George? Sure, sure. We both went to Tuxedo van at the same time. That boy in those late days, huh? I know George talks about it. I didn't know you were still in the van. I forgot about it. I guess George just told me.
Were there any other personnel changes later on, around 1930, earlier? Oh, I don't know. In Celestine. Oh, yeah, the pilot police.
This thing still isn't going very well. We didn't get those changes. You should try saying something to somebody over in front.
Go ahead, Chick. You do the talking. It's your recording.
Just going and talking about the days and...
Well, when I left the van...
I don't believe this is catching it loud enough.
I don't know. It's disgusting. When I left... Yeah, go ahead. When I left in 1930, Joshua Frazier took my place.
Oh, yeah. Sa'i we call him, huh?

Yeah, Sa'i. That's right. Married my cousin. Well, he took my place and three weeks afterwards, he comes to my house. He brings my drums back where I left over there for him to play on. He told me like, yes, he said, Cha'i. Say, how you do the... How you do the whole up the band like you did? I said, why? What's wrong with it? He said, didn't you like it? He said, yeah, but... Oh, man, I can't make that. He said, he played 22 quarters of high society and then told me to go out hot. So I told him I just couldn't make it. I couldn't go out hot. He said, what Chinese used to do? He said, well, I can't help what Chinese used to do. I can't do it. So he come to my house and asked me was I willing to go back. I told him, no, you keep the job. So after that, well, I don't know who took my... who took his place. Later after, well, Barbara took Sa'i's place after him. I hadn't left the band and then Sa'i took my place and then half the hour and go back, I think, to Barbara.
Well, just one second. Let me try one other...

This Kazir boy, he was playing tenor. I don't know, I was talking on tape to Bill one night and I could never figure... I know Bill Matthews was still there too. Yeah, he stood there, didn't change trombone. He came afterwards.
Huh? Yeah, he came after... you came in when they came in. Yeah, but I came in with God. With God. Yeah. That's how I said. Yeah. See, because on the record we used to record. Yeah.
And it took God's record. Well, yeah, but you see, I mean, after... I left him to go with Sam Morgan and Kimber took my place.
Took you place, yeah. Yeah.
Yeah, left hand Kimber, yeah. Took you place. Yeah, that was a long before he married you. To Ta Ta Daddy? Yeah.
So, Chani, you were telling us about, a minute ago, about up at Tulane, that you used to play some of the fraternities or the different games or what did you play for?
Yeah, different games. Football games. Yeah, I was 23. We went to Seawanna, Tennessee with him. And then we went to Kessler Field with him.
Which band was that?
It's Celestans.
Tell us that. It was very well received, huh? Very well received.
It was very well received. One of the boys took sick and never did get well. They were playing saxophone.
Who was that?
Willard Toomey. He was crippled for him. Walked like P. Ruff.
Yeah.

And after him, then Paul Barnes came. No, Adolph Alexander. Adolph Alexander. This is Junior. Adolph Alexander's younger. He came. On sax? On sax. Yeah. And after Adolph Alexander, then came Paul Barnes. Paul Barnes took his way.

Oh, you were talking a minute ago when the machine was off that sometimes there's a little hard feeling, maybe trouble between the uptown and downtown. Was there much rivalry? Yeah, it was real rivalry.
Yeah, it was real rivalry.
Between uptown and downtown. Yeah, plenty of that. Did you usually play at the downtown? I know you lived downtown, I guess, most of your life, didn't you? Yeah.

Well, you see, what the fellas didn't seem to understand is to hold the prejudices against each other. So, like if you were from downtown and you played with uptown, the fellas from downtown wouldn't hire you. Same way with the fellas uptown. They didn't like that, they'd fall from uptown playing with the downtown band. Was it that way all the time? All the time, yes. All the time.
Was the music much different? Did you feel as much difference between the musicians?
No, there wasn't no difference at all. It just was the question of who you like to be with.
Yeah, I thought maybe some people told me years, maybe way back even before your time, that they might have played a little rougher style uptown and more blues or something.
Well, you had the same thing on each section of the town.
Same thing, same type of music?

It's just the type that the fellas felt that because you from one neighborhood, you should stick in that neighborhood. A lot of times it wouldn't be for your playing that they wouldn't hire you. Just didn't like the idea you being with a different group. You know what I'm saying? They figure that you should be with your people because they were raised.
Yeah, I see.
And that would make a lot of time. It wouldn't be for your playing quality that they wouldn't hire you.
Yeah, I understand.

Playing time they could give you a job, but they wouldn't hire you on account of just having their preface against you. You know what I mean? Yeah. But for your playing quality, well, just like I said, you had good, best and better all over the world. Just was that animosity that they had for each other. Yeah. You understand what I mean?

I was going to ask if there's any more about the old time drummers. You mentioned Zeno. Was there much more you could tell us about Henry Zeno? I never did know much about him. Well, he was a great drummer. A really great drummer. He was the one you called A number one, didn't he? Huh? Which one was he you called A number one? You seemed to talk about... A number one?
Yeah.
You talked like McMurray once. McMurray. Yeah. Was he your favorite?
Favorite, my favorite. Favorite as all. My favorite. Next to him came Lloyd Contra. Next to him I was in the Suppan.
Yeah.
Those were the men I used to practice.
You mentioned you didn't have any lessons, but you were telling also when our tape was off a minute ago how people used to help one another.
Yeah, they did that a lot.
You just ask them questions and show you things?

That's the way I learned to music. Different fellas are all of them, well I'd go to different ones. Ask who they think is right. Well, if three of them tell me this fella's right and I don't say this fella's right, well I'll go ask somebody else. Well, I figure out of four out of five somebody's got to be right. Majority wins. Majority wins. That's the way I took them. That's the real facts about that. Now plenty of people don't understand it, but that's the truth from here to heaven.
I believe it.
See?
That's a good system. What have you been doing the last couple of years?
The last couple of years? Yeah. I haven't done anything. I just go around and the fellas ask me to play, but they try to get me back into it and I just wouldn't go back.
Do you have your drum set anymore? No. All right. I don't know that we got your address where you're living now.
We have it on.
Yes, I certainly do. We'll put that on another little slip later on we fill out. So I can contact you again in case you find Sonny Petit or some of the other fellas too.
Well I'll find him to see him.
Do you know where he's living now? Didn't he used to live over near Tom Anderson?

No, he don't live by Tom no more. He lives down in Gentellin. He lives way down in Gentellin. Somebody told me he's living in a trailer, way back in the Blue Boots. That's where he lives at. Way down in the trailer. Oh, if he lives in the trailer or what, I do not know. That's the way they do it to me. But I know how easy to find him because I know where his people live at down there.

You know, chick, what I was trying to figure out how they call that boy that lost his mind. Used to sing in the band with us. I was talking to Bill one night, never could think of the talk. Joe Lawrence. Joe Lawrence. That's it. Yeah. Boy used to sing in the band with Papa Sulla said, lost his mind.
He lost his mind. Joe Lawrence. Died. Died in Jacksonville.
Yeah, that's right.
Yeah, you're a nice singer.
Yeah.
Great singer.
Yeah. That's right.
Great singer. Plenty of pep to the time. Mm-hmm.
Joe Lawrence.
I just couldn't bring that man to mind. Yeah, he was great. Strong voice and power. Hey, he could sing any kind of numbers, you know. Don't care what time is it. Yeah.
Can you tell us any more about the Salistan style? I mean, did he always play sort of a sweet style with the old band? Always did.
Always did.
In late years when I heard him, he was playing regular Dixieland style.
Yeah, he was playing regular Dixieland style.
I wondered in the old days.
But he was a better straight trumpet player than he was a jazz trumpet. Dixieland.

Did he use mutes very much? Yeah, he was playing the mutes. It sounds like it on the old records, like he's using a mute all the time, or some of the time. Station calls and stuff. Yeah. If he usually had a mute in, or if that was just the way his tone sounded?
Well, practically that's his tone. Without the mute.
Without the mute.
Yeah.
Sometimes it's difficult on the record to tell if a fellow has a mute on, or if that's just the way his tone sounds.
But the more he used was, you know the kazoo horns? Oh yeah. That's what he used to use mostly for a mute. Oh yeah. The other way he supported him in between his fingers like that.
Was he using a mute on My Josephine? Yeah. That station calls was a big tune, wasn't it for you? Yeah, it was. Really big. I mean outside of the record it was a big tune.
Yeah. That's what the number hit for a tune. That and Whenever You're Lonesome. Whenever You're Lonesome. Yeah. That's another one of his real hit tunes. Whenever You're Lonesome just telephone me.
Oh yeah. Yeah. Well you were mentioning on the takes with shots that there were more made that weren't released. Is that right?
Yeah, that's right.
Do you happen to remember any of those tunes? Yeah. Which ones that weren't released? Uh, Alamazone.
That was made with the old blues. Yeah, the old blues. Never did come out.
Yeah, I never heard of it. I think Butter Beans and Suzie made an AZ blues.
Yes. Yeah. They did. But not your band. No. I mean that didn't come out. No.
Yeah. I figured they must have made more than those three pieces, but I wonder. Yeah.
Was Ralph Pierre the old fake guy, was he doing the recording?
Yeah. Yeah. Well he was a nice guy, wasn't he? Yeah, he was very nice. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Well he was a nice guy, wasn't he? Yeah, he was very nice.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.

Yeah, he was very nice. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah, because the last records we made, we made four records. And I haven't heard but three of them. Yeah. The last records we made, we made four. I've only heard of three.
There's four.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.

later though? Amazon. As you like it? As you like it and that AZ. It was right there, that AZ. Amazon never did come out. Was Schatz with the regular band or was he just hired for the... Well that was before the band split up. Oh yeah. And then he went over? I went with Celestine. He was risen. I was in Jacksonville, Florida. When I came back, I went to Celestine. See there's uh... those first four records, that was a full tuxedo band. And those other three records, those records were made after the band had split up.
Had you ever made any other records with any other band besides Celestine? Yeah. With the White Carnations.
The White Carnations. Oh. Do you remember the label? No, I think it was uh... Oak Hill, I think. Oak Hill. Was it made here in town? No, it was Jacksonville, Florida.
Oh. Who was with that group?

Uh... Henry Benedict. In fact, the whole band was uh... from out of town. Yeah. George Washington made two records. That's what I thought, yeah. George Washington played trombone on two of the records.
He played pretty gutty style? Yeah, it was good. Yeah. Yeah, very good. I know he plays modern now.

Yeah, it was very good. But he come up good. Here's another one that's come up, you know. During the time that when jazz was just getting famous real good. He got the four ways to have what he called. Ragtime. Bowel Hall. And there wasn't long in the 20's then it came jazz. And after the jazz then it came sophisticated. Swing and then after the swing then we got the B.Y.J. yesterday.
Now I know that George Washington doesn't even mention that he was here now, you know, because of the uh...status thing. He's got status. Oh yeah.
Yeah. Well I didn't know. But he will after I mentioned the white carnation. Yeah. He played him many years with Buddy Petit, you know. Yeah. Many years with Buddy Petit.
Yeah. It has this picture taken of Buddy Petit. That's right. It's a picture with the Edmund Hall.
Edmund Hall, yeah that's right.
Buddy Mandalay on banjo.
On banjo and uh... Clippard on drums. Chester was on... Chester was on bass. Yeah. And uh...Edmund Hall on clarinet. Yeah. Yeah. Say I'm at Mahal that's playing with Louis Armstrong.
You heard anything from Chester lately? He's still up there. No I haven't heard from George.
George might could tell you about that. No he out in some country town.
That's all I know. New Iberia or some place out near there. New Iberia. His uh...brother got a little sweet shop right uh...

Two, three doors from the Musicians Union, you know. Yeah. And I'm always asking him about him, but all he'd tell me is in the country I'm in. Yeah. Well he must be doing good out there. He don't come to the city. Those Florida bands were they pretty close to the style here in the city? Or were they more uh...rough? Some of them. Some of them. Yeah. But it was sort of similar to them.
Similar yeah. But that was...
Wasn't much... Wasn't much... The Cole Brothers band, the circus band, has a big...good name in there. Yeah.

But they played more music than the fellas was playing here. Yeah. The fellas there was playing more hit music, you understand. Yeah. In other words uh...whatever comes to their mind that's what they would make.
I know that George was telling me about when uh...Johnny Dunn came through there.
Yeah.

It's a big time. So did you say that George was still living? Yes. Yeah. Yeah. He's in pretty good shape too. What way is he in San Francisco? No. In Los Angeles. No. That's what you call it. Yeah. Still playing? Yeah. But he's got status. I thought...I thought he was dead. It's the same guy and he described him the same way he looks.
Same size as me. How old was he when you were there? He was about as long as my age. That's right. Same age. Same age as me.

I just thought he was dead. I know uh...little pills used to play with him too. Yeah. The cripple pill. The cripple pill. He died and uh... He died. Well of course uh...hab he's still uh...alive? Oh yeah. I mean he doesn't necessarily have to be dead. Yeah. But I mean the rumor was out that he was dead. You know what I mean? The way I heard it. Well he might as well be dead as far as New Orleans jazz is concerned. Oh yeah. Yeah. Yeah. He was playing with... He was playing with...
He was playing with...

Well he played with uh... Johnny Otis' rock and roll group for a while. Yeah. And uh...right now George Probert, the old fake clarinetist uses him occasionally. I think Elton can tell you about it. Elton's you know... Who? Pernell.
Yeah.
I'll see him I'll have to find out. Anybody else have a name that you...
No. I mean... Was there much difference in the old time drum style in regards to uh... The number of beats a major they hit?
Yeah a lot. A lot.
When they play nowadays?
A lot.
Was it uh...common for the uh... Banjo to stroke right with your wood blocks all the time? Always.
Always. Always. Did you usually use two beats or four beats to uh... Measure?

Well it depends how you felt about it. But the most... The only difference I find of uh... Of today because just like I told you... When... When the jazz and stuff were out... The fellas played card until they feel it. Yeah.
You understand?

Whatever sound the best to him. You understand what I mean? Some fellas would use four four beats like they do now. Yeah. Some would use the one two beats. Plenty fellas played on a lot of down beats. A lot of them played on up beats. A lot of them played on up beats.
Uh...
I'll tell you the difference of uh... Of the old style drumming and the drumming of today. The fellas beat more cymbals than they do drums.
Today?
Today. Yeah. And half of the fellas don't roll on their drums.
Oh that's true.
Half of them can roll. Okay. They don't practice rolling.
What about the sound of the snare? Was it crisp or more dull than it is now?
Crisp. Very crisp. More crisper than it is now. Crisp or now? Now cause they get that... That feel drum playing there now.
Yeah.
Deeper drums. Well that don't have anything to do with it.
What about tuning the drums? That's it.
That's it. That's it.
Higher attention.

Higher attention. See myself always tune my bass drum up enough. And tune my bass drum in D. Throw the snares off it. And get my D from a guitar player or a banjo player. Or either a bass player. Drums are in C aren't they? When they're natural. When they're natural. Yeah. But as it is though. A lot of people don't seem to believe it. But you're supposed to tune the drums just like you're tuning in the other instruments. Yeah.
They take something in F and try to get F out of the...

Exactly. And then... See like when uh... Years back. See like you have your snares on the drum. Well you walk across the floor and you could hear them snares ring. Yeah. And notice the fellas up to date don't tune drums like that. Yeah. In other words just like you take a... Cardboard and get there and go... Yeah. That's where you put it... That's where you... That's where you... That's where I tune my mouth snare from. That was... But... Close by being deep that don't have nothing to do with that. Yeah. It's according to how you set your snare.
It's a shame that you couldn't hear the drums on the old records. You know? There was that much going on. No.
Because when you would hit the drum they blanked the whole record. Yeah. That's why they used to use... All wood blocks in the... All wood blocks.
You used the bass drum too didn't you on a record?
No. No. Then used the bass drum at all. Or used the bass drum. No bass drum. No bass drum. You weren't using that.
You weren't using the stock then were you then?
No. So it wouldn't take on the record.
Yeah.

Nothing but the... Charney block and the cymbals. That's all. If you hit the drum they would just blank the whole record. Yeah. Wouldn't hear nothing. That's why you see all the old records, you have blocks on them, they don't have no drums.
You suppose that bugged the guys when they played? Huh? You suppose that bothered the guys when they played?
No, it didn't bother the guys, it just wouldn't take on the record.
No, but I mean with that absence of that drumming.

Well, no. You see, because you be beaten on the floor. You see, you put a pad on each other. They could hear that. They could feel the jolt, you understand what I mean? But the drum itself, you wouldn't play the drum. It was jolly, blanked the whole record. Just in the later years, well, after they improved the machines, well, they started recording the drums.
You never made any other records then besides the Salistan and the Carnations, those were the old-night records that you made?
That's all.
How many records did the Carnations then make?
Four, five.
Remember any of the numbers? They might be under another name or something sometime. Well, that's it.
I couldn't tell.
The title, the pieces.

We had one of the Sand City Blues. I remember Sand City Blues. And, uh, Sand City Blues. And Out on the Lake Breeze. And, uh, what is that number? I don't know, but, uh, Puppet Grindstone. Puppet Grindstone. Puppet Grindstone. Puppet Grindstone. I don't know.
Go watch for those. I don't think I've ever seen them, though, anyplace. Yeah.
Well, that was an unusual name for a band at a white carnation. I've never read of them. I've seen one of the records and I just passed it by.
Yeah. Really? Yeah. Remember what label? OK. OK label. The old OK.

Yeah. And then I'll tell you something else. You see, years back, you'd be playing the time you record records and you never, a lot of records was made and never were, I mean, you know, they changed names for them and then sometimes probably would steal the records. Yeah.
Yeah.
For the modeling somebody else's name. For the modeling somebody else's name.
Yeah. Exactly. You know, white carnation style was pretty much like Celestan? Or more?
More like P-rock. Oh. More like P-rock. More like P-rock.
There was no violin on it though, was there?
Yeah. There was.
There was.
All those bands up there used violin. Big trombone. Yeah. They were using two trombones in the band before we were using two trombones and things down there. That 16 piece band up there.

One question I was going to ask, how you used to sit on the stand when you'd be on those balconies, you know, like say, at Economy Hall or Hope's Hall. What was the order of the instruments? Where did you sit with your drums? Were you on one end? On the right hand.
On the right hand side and bass on the left hand side.
The bass over on the other hand. Yeah.
And who was next to you? Trombone.
Trombone. And then what?
Clarinet. Clarinet. Violin. Guita. Bass. Bass.
When you recorded it, it was a cellar stand band, did you sit in about that order or did they have you sit different?
No, it was set around. Sort of around. Put the drum on the way on the last in the back of the band.
Yeah.
The band would be up front, the drum being the, the drum and the bass being the back.
Yeah. That is done down at the Gottschalk building. Yeah.
Hmm. Gotcha. Right down on the Canal and Chop.

Yeah. Right down here, yeah. Five blocks down. Yeah. I was going to ask a little bit about the old John Robichaux band. You said that was one of your very first jobs, you remember. Yeah. Do you remember how Robichaux played violin? I understand he was a left-handed violin. Left-hand violin player. Was he very good at it or just ordinary? Do you remember much about it?
No, he was very good. Only one thing I hate about him. He rehearsed one number when you get in the pit he's play something else.
That's to see if he could catch his sleep.
Yeah, lots of times he'd do that.
Yeah, I guess.
Rehearsed one, or you know, one number, you're expecting to go back and play that number, when you get in there he's throwing something else up.
Mm-hmm.
It's kind of nervous too, you understand what I mean? Yeah. Couldn't talk back to him.
No, you wouldn't be able to. How was Manuel Perez as the leader? You were just a little boy, you say, when you played with him. Yeah. Very fine man.
Very nice to you and all?
Very fine man. Very fine man. Very fine man.
Very fine man. He had no bad habits whatsoever. He didn't drink, he was a cigar maker and didn't smoke.
That's funny.
Never know him to gamble or nothing. I doubt it, never know him to chase no women's or nothing. Straight man. Straight man. Drink plenty lemonade and eat plenty cake.
I knew him before he died but didn't get to know him well.

Well really to get to tell you the facts truth about it, our school, Paul Boyer's sister. Oh yes. She gave a concert at the economy hall. It's like I told you, I always could play ever since I know myself. Nobody taught me that I always could play. So, the band was downstairs eating supper and drinking. Manny Perez, myself was upstairs in the balcony. So, I told him I know how to play drum. He said, you sure you know how to play drum? I said, yes. So, he took his, we called him Connett at that time.
Yes.
So, he took his Connett and the number he played was, you made me love you and I didn't want to do it. But you know that number come out way back here in 1908.
Yeah, then he came back a few years ago. Yeah, he got to come back new.

He been out two, three times since then. Yeah. This was in 1908. I was nothing, my feet couldn't, I used to have to put a set on a little stool like that. Well, you can sell it from my size there now for my feet to reach the thing. Yeah. So, while the band was eating supper, him and I was up there. So, he ran over the number. I played it good, that's all. And Bill Maffia's brother was playing drum with him then, the one he called BB. And he come back up there and he said, I got a surprise for you. So, I said, what's a surprise? He said, there's something mighty funny, you got a surprise. He used to call him Mix, you know. I said, you see that little kid there? He said, that little kid going to be a good drummer. He said, let him play a number. I told him, man, that little boy can't play nothing, nothing, that little boy going to play with a big band. He said, he just now got through a play. He said, if he make a mistake, he said, I'll be responsible for the question. He said, oh, well, he hit off two beats there and I just went on in with the drum. I just went on and I played. I said, after that, I played another number. After another number. Well, after that, well, when any of those old man would take sick, well, they figured that they had more chance to get me. They said, well, go get that little boy. You see? Well, they figured nine o'clock at night I'm in bed, you know, because at that time, well, the old people were strict. Children didn't run the street. You know, like late hours like they do now. Well, those old man there, well, they would, they'd come get me in the buggy or eat in the carriage. They didn't have no automobile like they have now, you know. They'd come get me in the carriage or eat in the buggy. Tell my mama that they'd look out for me.
Yeah.
But I'd go in and that's how I got to playing with all those older men that's way ahead of my time would make people think that I'm older than what I am.
Yeah, I thought you were way older than you are.
Yeah. I said, that's how I got to know those men and know their style. Well, just like I told you all, I was always interested in music.
You were young on the Celestines too then. Huh? You were pretty young on the Celestines.
Oh yeah, way young on the Celestines. Yeah. So. About 24, 20? When I went with Celestines I was exactly 18 years old. So you went there around 1919 or so?
Yeah. When came first?

Well, I had played with them but I mean I was in a regular band like I told you. When I was a kid there, that's how I knew them fellas like Reddy Keppel and Bunk and them. Well, I know them fellas that when I was a little boy, you see. Well, those fellas go around and they be playing those dances like that. They'd all say, let that little kid play something. I didn't play a number like that. People would, they'd hear the drum playing but they couldn't, they'd bark and they're already high and they couldn't see me behind the drum. They'd see me behind the drum and people would come up and see me. They'd come there and I'd pick up hats full of money. I'd make more than what the band would be making. That's how I know all them old fellas.

Well, I think that covers most of your life pretty well. We don't want to keep you here all afternoon. I know you've been talking a long time so I think there's just about two here. Unless there's something else you want to add that you can think of about your life and music?
Well, that's about all.
